The quiet return of the home server

Cheap storage, better containers and a backlash against subscriptions have pushed self-hosting from a weekend hobby to a daily habit. Across forums and group chats, people describe the same arc: a spare machine, a few containers, and then a slow realisation that most of the services they pay for each month can run in a closet.

The tools have matured. Container platforms with friendly web interfaces handle updates, backups and permissions, and a single small box can serve media, photos, documents and a password manager to a whole household without any of it leaving the house.

What has changed most is the audience. It is no longer only people who enjoy configuring things; it is people who are tired of price rises, shutdowns and terms of service that change under them. For them, the appeal is control rather than tinkering.

There are trade-offs. You become your own support desk, and a power cut or a failed disk is your problem to solve. But for a growing number of households that feels like a fair price for owning their own corner of the internet.
